tldr: A meta agent (GPT-4o) programs new agents as complete `forward()` Python functions, scores each on a validation slice, and feeds the growing scored archive back into its own prompt — discovering designs that beat hand-designed baselines on DROP, MGSM, MMLU and GPQA.
method: The search space is Python, not prompts. The meta agent is handed a <100-line framework (`Info` namedtuple; `FM_Module` wrapping role/model/temperature and a `query()` that concatenates Info objects into a structured prompt) and must write one complete `def forward(self, taskInfo)` per candidate, which the harness executes. Loop (Algorithm 1): seed the archive with hand-designed baselines (COT, COT-SC, Self-Refine, LLM Debate, Quality-Diversity, Step-back, Role Assignment); the meta agent sees the full scored archive plus 'WRONG Implementation examples' and emits {thought, name, code}; two self-reflection rounds revise it for interestingness, implementation mistakes and improvement; it is evaluated on the domain validation split; runtime errors trigger up to five debug reflections; the agent and its metric are appended to the archive. Search runs independently per domain; one fixed meta agent (gpt-4o-2024-05-13) proposes while every candidate and baseline is scored by gpt-3.5-turbo-0125.
results: Table 1 (held-out test, 95% bootstrap CI): DROP F1 79.4 ± 0.8 vs best hand-designed 65.8 ± 0.9 (Role Assignment) and prompt-only OPRO 69.1 ± 0.9 — the paper's headline +13.6; MGSM accuracy 53.4 ± 3.5 vs 39.0 ± 3.4 (LLM Debate), +14.4; MMLU 69.6 ± 3.2 vs 65.9 ± 3.2 (COT-SC); GPQA 34.6 ± 3.2 vs 31.6 ± 3.2 (Self-Refine) — the gap shrinks where FM knowledge, not scaffolding, caps performance.

ARC (25 search iterations, 20-question validation / 60-question test, 5 evaluations each): top three discovered agents reach 13.7 / 13.3 / 12.7 % on GPT-3.5 vs best baseline 8.0 (LLM Debate); transferred unchanged to Claude-Sonnet they reach 38.7 / 39.7 / 48.3 % vs 31.7 baseline (Table 3).

Zero-shot transfer of the top-3 MGSM agents within math (Table 4): GSM8K 69.5 ± 3.2 vs best baseline 43.6 ± 3.4 (+25.9), GSM-Hard 31.2 ± 3.2 vs 18.0 ± 2.7 (+13.2), SVAMP 82.6 vs 78.5, ASDiv 91.8 vs 89.2. Beyond math (Table 5) DROP F1 70.4–71.9 vs 65.8 and MMLU 62.4–67.0 vs 65.9, but GPQA 28.6–29.9 stays under the 31.6 baseline — 'outperform or match', not a clean sweep.

Empty-initialization ablation (Table 6): with no seeded baselines Meta Agent Search still beats every hand-designed baseline in all four domains, and in math it beats its own seeded run (MGSM 67.5 ± 3.3 vs 53.4 ± 3.5), while seeding wins elsewhere (DROP 79.4 vs 73.9; MMLU 69.6 vs 68.5; GPQA 34.6 vs 32.7).
Cost (Appendix J): ~$500 per ARC search-and-evaluation run and ~$300 per reasoning-domain run, dominated by gpt-3.5-turbo-0125 evaluation calls rather than meta-agent proposals.
advantages: Whole-program search space: because the candidate is arbitrary Python, the loop learns prompts, workflows, ensembles, criticism and refinement together. The prompt-only baseline OPRO is beaten in all four domains (DROP 69.1 vs 79.4), which is the paper's direct evidence that code-space ADAS buys more than prompt optimization.

The stepping-stone story is documented, not asserted: on ARC a 'multiple COTs → refine → ensemble' pattern emerged at iteration 3 and was reused afterwards, and the best agent combined ideas first seen at iterations 5 (diverse feedback), 11 (trait-specific experts) and 12 (human-like critic) — LLM-mediated crossover over an archive rather than hill-climbing on one incumbent.

Generalization is measured three ways, not one: transfer to unseen math domains, to non-math domains, and across four FMs (GPT-3.5, Claude-Haiku, GPT-4, Claude-Sonnet), where the searched agents keep their lead at every model — evidence the discovered designs are not overfit to the searching model.

Extremely cheap substrate: <100 lines of framework, API-only, no GPUs, and the outputs are readable Python — the paper argues this makes the search space interpretable and auditable in a way graph/network search spaces are not.
limitations: One objective (performance) only: cost, latency and robustness are not optimized; multi-objective ADAS is left to future work, and the ~$300–500 per run is itself never treated as a search constraint.

By the authors' own account the evaluation function is the weak link — evaluating on a validation split and reading a scalar is 'both expensive and overlooks valuable information', discarding the run logs that carry failure modes, and it cannot handle subjectively judged tasks.

Scope is single-step QA plus ARC-style grid puzzles; multi-step interaction with real environments is untested, and the meta agent itself is fixed — the paper never improves the meta-agent's own prompt or search policy, listing self-referential 'Higher-order ADAS' explicitly as future work.
Where the FM lacks the knowledge, agent design cannot compensate: the GPQA/MMLU gains are small (34.6, 69.6) and the transferred math agents fall below the GPQA baseline (28.6–29.9 vs 31.6).
fits: Stage 5 (Harness-level RSI), the cleanest anchor of the Prompt & Program Optimization group: the evolving artifact is a whole agent program while the improver stays fixed. Successors (DGM, HyperAgents, AutoHarness, Continual Harness, MetaSkill-Evolve) extend the loop to the meta level or to online settings. Pairs with OPRO, Promptbreeder, STOP and DSPy as its prompt-only ancestors.
reading: §3 (the four-step loop), §4.1–4.3 with Tables 1–3 for the numbers, Appendix B (prompts, the two Reflexion rounds, the error-reflection prompt), H (pseudocode), I (empty-init ablation), J (cost); Appendix G for discovered agents' code.
